planting.note: Set divisions into humus-rich leaf litter under oak-juniper canopy in part shade; keep evenly moist through spring bloom, then let the soil dry as the plant goes summer-dormant.

directions: Plateau spiderwort is an Edwards Plateau endemic that carpets the leaf litter of oak-juniper canyon woodlands, sending up clusters of three-petaled blue-violet flowers each morning in spring before the foliage withers back with summer heat and drought. It spreads slowly from fleshy roots into loose clumps and is best propagated by dividing established clumps in late winter or early spring rather than from seed. Site it in filtered light beneath trees in humus-rich, limestone-derived soil, and avoid summer irrigation once it has gone dormant, since rot is more likely than drought stress. It pairs naturally with other Hill Country woodland-floor species such as cedar sedge and wild petunia.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings on rocky, well-drained limestone slopes or along a fence line in full sun; allow the vine to trail over boulders or train it onto a trellis since it climbs by tendrils.

directions: Sweet mountain grape is a small-leaved, drought-hardy grape endemic to limestone canyons and rocky bluffs of the Edwards Plateau and Trans-Pecos, far less vigorous than cultivated table grapes and well suited to steep, poor soils where little else will grow. Its tiny purple-black grapes ripen in late summer and are intensely tart fresh but make a prized wild jelly, while also feeding mockingbirds, cardinals, and other wildlife. Because it tolerates thin, rocky, alkaline soil and needs no irrigation once established, it is valued for erosion control on Hill Country slopes as much as for fruit. Give it full sun and sharp drainage, and let it scramble naturally over rock or shrubs rather than forcing it onto a tight trellis.

planting.note: Transplant into rocky, well-drained soil in dappled shade beneath canyon rim vegetation; water in well and keep lightly moist the first season, then rely on natural rainfall.

directions: Wright's boneset is a semi-woody subshrub of limestone canyons in the Trans-Pecos and western Edwards Plateau, growing in the dappled shade of canyon walls and juniper-oak slopes where it is more heat- and drought-tolerant than its showier relative, white mistflower. Its small, deeply veined fan-shaped leaves give rise to flat-topped clusters of fuzzy white flowers in fall, drawing a heavy flush of queen butterflies, monarchs, and native bees during migration season. In zone 7 it often freezes back to the base in hard winters but resprouts reliably from the woody crown each spring. Prune lightly in late winter to maintain a tidy shape and encourage dense fall bloom.

planting.note: Wedge divisions or small plugs into thin, gritty soil pockets among limestone rock in part sun; sharp drainage matters far more than soil fertility.

directions: Fairy swords is an unusually sun-tolerant fern found rooted in limestone and igneous rock crevices across the Edwards Plateau and Trans-Pecos, where most true ferns cannot survive the exposure. The undersides of its narrow, pinnately divided fronds are coated in dense star-shaped scales that give the foliage a silvery cast and help it curl and desiccate during drought, reviving fully within a day or two of rain. It bears no flowers and holds purely textural, rock-garden value, thriving in crevice gardens and dry-stacked limestone walls with morning sun and afternoon shade. Avoid rich garden soil or regular irrigation, both of which cause it to decline.

planting.note: Plant container stock in well-drained, limestone-derived soil in the dappled shade of oak-juniper canopy; water through the first year to establish, then rely on rainfall.

directions: Switch-leaf barberry is a narrow Edwards Plateau endemic shrub, often mistaken for its common cousin agarita but distinguished by broader, less rigidly spined leaflets and a stronger tolerance for shaded canyon understory conditions. Clusters of small bright-yellow flowers open in late winter, followed by tart red berries in late spring that make a jelly nearly indistinguishable from agarita jelly and are relished by birds. Because it tolerates deeper shade than agarita, it fills a niche along canyon walls and beneath dense juniper-oak canopy where the sun-loving agarita struggles. Give it rocky, alkaline, well-drained soil and avoid wet feet, especially in winter.

planting.note: Direct sow or transplant into well-drained soil in full sun to light shade after danger of frost; established plants need no supplemental water and self-sow readily.

directions: Toothleaf goldeneye is a tall, fast-growing perennial sunflower relative native to the Edwards Plateau, South Texas brush country, and northern Mexico, erupting into masses of small bright-yellow daisy flowers from late summer through fall. It is one of the most important late-season nectar sources for migrating monarchs and other pollinators in Hill Country gardens, blooming after most other wildflowers have faded. In colder Hill Country winters it typically freezes back to the ground but resprouts vigorously from the base in spring; cutting it back hard in late winter keeps plants dense rather than leggy. It tolerates poor, rocky, caliche soils and thrives with minimal care once established.
